title: Could Homework Widen the Gap Between Families?
paragraphs: Few features of primary schooling are as taken for granted as homework, but a new paper from the University of Manchester suggests that the routine may be reinforcing the very inequalities schools hope to narrow. Published in the British Journal of Sociology of Education, the study examines the expectations placed on parents' time in the relationship between home and school.

The authors rely on a detailed case study of one mother, Emma, who works until 8pm, and her child's teacher, Mrs Higgins; the first author was herself a parent at the school. Using Pierre Bourdieu's notion of cultural capital, they argue that time is an unevenly distributed resource. Families with more time, knowledge and money can supervise homework or pay for private tutoring, whereas others find the task stressful or even shaming, particularly when they lack confidence in the subject.

The researchers also caution that schools may mistake a shortage of time for a shortage of commitment, fostering a "deficit" view of some parents. Scrapping homework is no panacea, they add, since other forms of parental engagement could simply take its place. As Professor Laura Black puts it, the bigger challenge is to rethink what we expect from parents in the first place. A caveat is in order: a single case cannot speak for every school, and the release does not mention funding.

questions.q: What is the study's central argument?
questions.a: Homework may reinforce inequality because families have unequal time and resources.

questions.q: Why do the authors say that abolishing homework is no panacea?
questions.a: Other forms of parental engagement could replace it.

questions.q: What caveat applies to the findings?
questions.a: They rest on a single case study, so they cannot speak for every school.
